title: Nested loop
body:
Example 3
two loops
```C++
for (int row = 0; row < ROWS; row++) {
	for (int col = 0; col < COLS; col++)
		cout << grid[row][col] << " ";
	cout << endl;
}
```

The inner loop runs **completely** for every single pass of the outer one, so the body executes
`ROWS * COLS` times. Printing a table, comparing every element against every other, and walking
a 2D [[Array]] are all this shape.

Two rules that stop most nested-loop bugs:

- **Each loop needs its own [[Control variable]].** Reusing `i` for both is the classic
  [[Logic Errors|logic error]].
- **Reset the inner one.** With `for` the initialiser does it every time; with a
  [[While loop]] you have to reset the counter yourself before the inner loop, inside the outer
  body, or the second pass finds it already past its limit and runs zero times.

The cost is the thing to notice: two nested loops over *n* items is $n^2$ work, which is fine at
10 and painful at 100000. Why that matters, and which algorithms avoid it, is [[Time Complexity]]
in [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]].
